touches.text: Owns the inspectors and gates (draft, moving from standalone): build_inspector, plan_inspector, ticket_inspector, corrosion, exemptions, rehearsal, determinism, import_sieve, and the tester (11; Q#33, Akien 2026-10-29). (Not diagnostic_inspector: it is base's, 17.3.) The code pipeline's inspectors and gates move to CodeMother; any that are not about code (if such existed) would not. (Q#31, Akien 2026-10-27)
Runs a proof as its own process and writes a validation record (claim, caller, date, method, verdict, evidence, falsifier, horizon).
Hollow runs: proves a proof goes red when the build is removed.
Seals: one current validation per proof, beside the proof. A seal holds while the code it measured is unchanged.
Test runs are transient (30 days, 4.3.2); seals are records of truth (git).
build_inspector: python sieves run after a build; reds a component that fails one (no charter, no proofs, a silent device, ...). "We find a new thing, we add a new sieve." → CodeMother (10.3.5)
The inspector outputs only its findings. It certifies nothing, records no crossing, and posts nothing; the gate consumes its findings (19.14.1).

ROOT INTENTION for checks and gates (Akien, 2026-10-27): the inspector does all the checks, so there is no need for more checks anywhere else. The inspector's output is consumed by the gate. The gate's output is the certificate. "This was how I meant it all along."

open_questions.text: What keeps the after-failure check from being a lock pick: a reader other than the builder (a cold cheap model, as rehearsal), the finding recording both whys verbatim and which lost, a pass that dies with its one ticket, a per-sieve count of passes that reds the sieve past some number? Which of these, or what else?
